prize_parts.citation: for the invention and development of the optical lattice clock, which brought the measurement of time to the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: I keep the optical lattice clock first, and the opening ballots strengthen that view. Five of eight members ranked it, three put it first, and nobody ranked it below second. That is unusual on a list where most candidates are contested. The achievement is a bounded invention. Katori's magic-wavelength condition removes the light shift that would otherwise ruin a trapped-atom clock. Ye's group then showed what the idea can do: stability and accuracy at the 10^-18 level, many-body operation with a spin-polarised Fermi gas, and centimetre-scale tests of gravitational time dilation. Independent clocks at JILA, Tokyo/RIKEN, PTB, NIST and SYRTE agree at that level, so there is no maturity question. The science also reaches beyond metrology, into searches for varying constants and dark matter and into the coming redefinition of the second. As an atomic theorist I know the supporting structure (polarisabilities, blackbody and higher-order light shifts, relativistic atomic structure) and I find the physics deep, not only the engineering. Two names are a clean attribution, and the citation can be written to exclude ion clocks and comb technology.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is credit and precedent. The 2005 prize covered the frequency comb and Wineland shared the 2012 prize for controlling single ions, so some will say precision optical metrology is already honoured. Ion-clock pioneers and the early Sr and Yb lattice groups are outside the two names, and a citation that is too broad would invite their claims. A second concern is that the redefinition of the second has not yet happened, so a prize could be read as anticipating a metrological decision instead of recognising a discovery. I think both concerns are manageable, but they are real.

responses.point: Kroll ranks B027 first but asks whether the committee should frame the prize around optical clocks generally, which could bring in ion-clock pioneers not on the credited list, and says the citation must be kept narrow.
responses.response: I agree with the narrow framing and would resist the broader one. A prize for optical clocks in general would make us adjudicate between neutral-atom and ion clocks, and Al+ and Yb+ clocks involve different people and a different physical argument. The magic-wavelength lattice is a specific idea with a specific demonstrator, and the 10^-18 result came from that route. The citation should name the lattice clock. I raised ion clocks as an uncertainty in my opening ballot and I now think it argues for the narrow wording, not for adding names.

responses.point: Pearce puts the IceCube neutrino discovery first, as a new observational window and the kind of discovery the prize has honoured, and ranks the lattice clock second with the caveat that others may claim a share.
responses.response: I take the IceCube case seriously. The diffuse flux is secure and neutrino astronomy is new. But Pearce's own attribution paragraph says the supplied pair may not capture the decisive contributors in a collaboration of hundreds, with AMANDA as predecessor, and that he cannot verify the division of credit. On the clock the same member sees little unresolved allocation. When two candidates are comparable in importance, I weight the cleaner attribution heavily, and here B027 is cleaner. On the early Sr and Yb groups, I think they built on Katori's concept and Ye's group did the decisive accuracy work. I would still welcome a view from the astroparticle side on whether Karle and Halzen are the right names.

responses.point: Johansson puts circuit QED first and the lattice clock second, arguing that circuit QED is the architecture behind most superconducting processors, while noting that its subject area is close to the 2025 prize.
responses.response: I respect the scale of circuit QED and Johansson's candour about the proximity to the 2025 prize. I disagree on ordering for two reasons. First, the 2025 prize on macroscopic quantum tunnelling in circuits makes a second superconducting-circuit award within a year hard to justify, and Johansson says so too. Second, the attribution is harder. Johansson, Kroll and Mehlig all note that Girvin and the wider Yale and ETH groups complicate the three-name set. Circuit QED is also better understood as an enabling architecture than as one discovery, whereas the lattice clock is a single invention with a clear measured result. I could support circuit QED in a later year if the committee wants a separate quantum-technology prize.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks the topological insulator candidate third and flags the overlap with the 2016 prize and the omission of Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang from the credited names, while placing DMFT first.
responses.response: Eriksson's attribution worry is the same one I have about B057, and it is why I rank it second, not first. Topological insulators are broadly agreed as important: seven members ranked them and four put them in the top three. But the HgTe proposers and the 3D contributors are missing from the three names, and Zhang is deceased. I would hold B057 as the leading alternative, but I would not trade the clean B027 for a prize whose credit we cannot settle. On DMFT, I accept that it is a major method, but only two members ranked it, so it does not have the breadth of support yet.

responses.point: Danielsson ranks B027 first, B057 second and IceCube third, and notes that the lattice clock needs separating from comb-related precedent and that clock-based redefinition of the second is pending but well advanced.
responses.response: I agree with Danielsson on the order of the top three, and I think the comb precedent is answered by the citation. The comb gave a way to count optical cycles. The lattice clock is a different thing: a way to hold many atoms in a state where the transition is not perturbed, which the comb does not provide. Nothing in the 2005 prize text covered that. The pending redefinition does not weaken the case, because the physics result is already independently established.

uncertainties: How far the committee thinks the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 prize for single-ion control already cover precision optical metrology.
Whether the early Sr and Yb lattice groups, or the ion-clock pioneers, have a claim that two names cannot represent.
Whether a two-part prize pairing B027 with B057 could be configured inside the three-person limit; with the credited names it cannot, so I propose B027 alone.
My recollection of priority dates and clock performance numbers is not checked against sources here.
statement.conflict_note: From my profile, my attosecond work involves collaborations with the Lund group, ETH Zurich (Keller) and others, and I am an atomic theorist, so I am in the same broad field as B027. My profile documents no collaboration with Katori or Ye, nor with any credited name in B057 or B032, so I do not see a specific recusal issue. I declare that field proximity and would recuse on any candidate involving the people named in my profile.
